title: Engineering \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two remote superconducting qubits via a multimode waveguide
abstract: Waveguides provide a flexible platform for long-range interactions between superconducting qubits. Here, we study how to engineer the effective \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions between two qubits via qubit frequency assignments and multimode interference determined by the mode configuration and standing-wave parities of a finite multimode waveguide. For a single-mode waveguide, we find that \(XY\) and \(ZZ\) interactions cannot be simultaneously suppressed to zero and the residual qubit-qubit coupling always exists. For example, the \(XY\) interaction may be suppressed to a negligible level when two qubits and the waveguide mode satisfy the two-photon resonant condition, but the \(ZZ\) interaction cannot be switched off. For multimode configurations within the central dispersive window, the engineered interaction types are very different for odd and even numbers of modes. Even-mode configurations can readily produce strong \(XY\) interactions, whereas odd-mode configurations can strongly suppress the \(XY\) interaction while retaining a finite \(ZZ\) interaction. Full-Hamiltonian simulations of minimal two- and three-mode configurations confirm \(XY\)-dominated SWAP dynamics and \(ZZ\)-dominated CZ-type dynamics, respectively. These results establish a frequency assignment criterion of qubits and waveguide modes for selectively engineering long-range qubit-qubit interaction types induced by the waveguide with finite multimode.
summary: This paper details the engineering of two-qubit interactions ($	ext{XY}$ and $	ext{ZZ}$) between superconducting qubits using a multimode waveguide. By exploiting multimode interference and controlling qubit frequencies relative to the waveguide's mode spectrum, the authors demonstrate a method to selectively tune the interaction type. This provides a crucial design criterion for building scalable quantum processors with tailored gate operations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of selectively engineering and controlling the effective two-qubit interactions ($	ext{XY}$ and $	ext{ZZ}$) between two remote superconducting qubits using a multimode waveguide.
main_result: It establishes a frequency assignment criterion based on the waveguide mode structure, showing that the interaction type can be selectively engineered to be $	ext{XY}$-dominated (for SWAP dynamics) or $	ext{ZZ}$-dominated (for CZ-type dynamics) by controlling qubit frequencies relative to the mode spectrum.
method: The analysis uses second-order perturbation theory to derive the effective $	ext{XY}$ interaction and numerical diagonalization of the full Hamiltonian to extract the $	ext{ZZ}$ interaction, focusing on multimode interference effects.
model_or_system: The system consists of two superconducting qubits coupled to a finite-length microwave transmission-line waveguide supporting discrete multimode standing-waves. The interaction is mediated by virtual photon exchange in the dispersive regime.
key_observables: Effective $	ext{XY}$ interaction strength ($J_{	ext{eff}}$) and $	ext{ZZ}$ interaction strength ($\zeta$).
important_parameters: Qubit frequencies ($\omega_1, \omega_2$), waveguide mode frequencies ($\omega_{r,m}$), and the standing-wave parities ($s_m$).
main_assumptions: The qubits are assumed to operate in the dispersive regime, meaning the detuning $|\Delta_{\mu m}|$ is much larger than the coupling strength $|g_{\mu m}|$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coupling of two transmons to a multimode waveguide, and one figure specifically shows the dependence of $J_{	ext{eff}}$ on two qubit frequencies relative to two neighboring modes, highlighting cancellation conditions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general Hamiltonian and coupling mechanism. It then derives the effective $	ext{XY}$ interaction via second-order processes and the $	ext{ZZ}$ interaction via higher-order terms. The core of the work involves analyzing how multimode interference, governed by mode parity and frequency detuning, allows for selective control over the ratio $|J_{	ext{eff}}|/|\zeta|$.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum information because it provides a detailed, physics-based blueprint for designing hardware architectures. The ability to switch between $	ext{XY}$ and $	ext{ZZ}$ coupling regimes using only frequency tuning is a critical requirement for implementing universal quantum gates.
